text:
没必要去争谁家模型强，我一路摸爬过来，说句实在的，绝大多数日常工作，用 GLM、DeepSeek、Kimi、Qwen，已经完全够了，写文案、做总结、改简历、整理资料、写脚本、做表格、拆方案，这些活儿其实没必要 Claude Sonnet、Fable、GPT 顶配。

但反过来，也要尝尝细糠是什么味儿，知道能力边界和差异在哪。

我现在，日常杂活，用便宜的国产模型，能完成 80 分就够了，不会为了 5 分的提升，多花 5 倍成本。

复杂的任务，需要深度思考的商业方案、深度推理、跨文档分析，用完了国产的再用顶级模型跑一遍，看它到底强在哪里。

所以争了半天谁强没啥意义，看兜里预算决定这才是我们最划算的用法。

不是每顿都吃米其林，很多时候楼下小馆子就能吃饱，还便宜。

但还是要至少试一次顶级模型。不是为了装，也不是为了跟风，而是你只有吃过细糠，才知道差距到底在哪里。

你会知道什么叫上下文稳定，什么叫复杂任务不跑偏，什么叫它真的理解你的意图，而不是只是在接话。

试过之后，你再用国产模型，心里就有数了。哪些活儿可以省钱，哪些活儿不能省，哪些任务必须上强模型，哪些任务根本没必要。

如果你能建立起自己的模型调度能力，便宜模型负责干粗活，强模型负责做判断，这才对路子。

如果你能看到这，关注我的人，没用过claude和codex顶级模型的，留个言，我去给你们搞一些免费的api回来。

关于无招，直接说几句大白话：

1、我一直很讨厌无招。特别是无招带队下的钉钉管理方式。这次无招下课，普天同庆。

2、同时我很讨厌阿里不少高管嘴里的“有情有义”。情义容易滋生关系，产生各种奇葩。大量组织僵化、劣币驱逐良币、嫡系文化等，都来自在商业组织里谈情义。

3、商业组织里的“无情无义”，往往是好事。这点特别佩服字节。虽然字节让人有很强的齿轮感、螺丝感，但因为“无情无义”没那么多，更多是看“数据”、看“逻辑”，反而很多地方是晴天，不会滋生乱七八糟的东西。

本不想得罪人，没想到之前的言论，引发了好多误解。干脆大白话。

往后不再评论任何关于无招的事。剧终。

OpenAI 核心产品负责人 Thibault Sottiaux 在接受《连线》采访时，自曝了当年从 Google DeepMind 愤而跳槽至 OpenAI 的内幕。Sottiaux 透露，在 2022 年底 ChatGPT 发布并点燃全球生成式 AI 浪潮之前，DeepMind 内部实际上早已掌握并「压箱底」了长达两年的类似大语言模型与对话技术，但当时并未选择将其推向公众。

Sottiaux 表示，2022 年 ChatGPT 的横空出世彻底启发了他，让他意识到自己不愿再守着技术却没有任何作为。他坦言：「这（大语言模型技术）是我们在 DeepMind 已经攥了（sitting on）差不多两年的东西，但我们当时就是没去行动。」这促使他决心搬到旧金山加入 OpenAI。在此之前，他曾在 Google 伦敦办公室工作，后加入 DeepMind 负责 AlphaGo 等项目的研究基础设施建设。

如今，Sottiaux 已升任 OpenAI 核心产品负责人，直接汇报给 Greg Brockman，全面主导 ChatGPT 的大改版以及与 Codex 智能体沙箱的融合。他透露，当前的底层技术已经成熟，OpenAI 计划在未来几周内将 Codex 融入 ChatGPT。他强调，公司更倾向于进行一系列小规模迭代发布，因为在变化极快的 AI 领域，没人能承受「搞出大新闻却发现做错了」的代价。

最近发生的事。。

我公司，有个94年的男孩追了个99年的女孩2年多，这个女孩嫌弃94的同事，年龄大了，又不会花言巧语提供情绪价值，一直没啥进度！！

然后三个多月前，女孩玩游戏，认识了00后的男孩（具体是02还是03年，不太清楚）一下上头了，认识2个多月就辞职，说和男朋友去创业，当初来辞职的时候，她的同事都说见过那个男孩，感觉不太靠谱的样子，而且现在创业也不太好，叫她注意，或者去创业不要辞职，有个退路，。那个时候女孩正在上头的时候，坚决辞职了，。，然后这个男同事，还颓废了几天！！

谁知道，过了一个多月，那个女孩找到我，又想回公司上班，说她被骗了，男孩给她积蓄全骗光，失联啦，而且创业租的办公公司，是以她的身份信息租的，签了三年，男孩才付了3个月房租，现在她要是退租，还被房主追讨违约责任！！

我正考虑的时候（本意不想答应，所以想拖下时间），这个94年的男孩来找我了，给那个女孩说好话，我问他们啥关系，他支支吾吾的不愿回答。。后面问急了，说那个女孩同意他的追求了。。

text:
世界只有两种人
一种是赢了的赌徒
一种是输了的赌徒
马斯克是前者

他的前半生就是一连串高风险下注

12岁自学编程卖出第一款游戏
17岁离开南非去加拿大，24岁创办Zip2，卖掉后赚到第一桶金。随后做https://t.co/QSlvU2qSuV，后来并入PayPal，eBay收购时，他拿走1.8亿美元

正常人到这已经躺平了，他没有

2002年他把钱砸进SpaceX，前三次发射失败，公司差点破产。2004年投Tesla，08年金融危机时两家公司同时缺钱，他个人财产接近归零。

然后第四次发射成功，SpaceX活了下来
Tesla也活了下来

后面的故事大家都知道了
Falcon 9回收火箭，Starship反复爆炸又反复重来，440亿美元买下Twitter改造成X，再往后是Neuralink、xAI、Optimus、Robotaxi……

马斯克每一把都梭哈
而且他好像真的能接受归零

你敢一直梭哈吗？？？

B站百万博主徐师傅最近访谈了一个曾经靠赌球赚了1000万，后面输光，妻离子散的一个大哥。

这个大哥人生犯了几个错误。

第二个是把运气当成实力，赢的时候，顺的时候，觉得自己很牛逼，输的时候，想加倍赢回来，结果越输越多，最后不仅自己亏光，还把父母的钱也输光。

他后来反思说，赌博的结局肯定是输光，无论怎么玩都是庄家赚钱。

text:
我觉得真正护城河最深的是 SpaceX。

因为不管是 Anthropic 还是 OpenAI，目前并没有真正决出胜负。大模型的迭代还在快速进展期，未来可以优化的空间非常大。

Anthropic、OpenAI 还有 Google 这三家领先的模型，再加上 Meta 也在狂追，以及 SpaceX 自己拥有的 Grok 模型（xAI），这五家未来的竞争态势其实是不清晰的。哪怕是排在后面的 Meta 和 SpaceX，未来也有后来居上的可能性。

但是不管模型怎么竞争，一个非常清晰的方向就是：未来对于算力的需求将是非常恐怖的。

在算力基础设施这一块，我觉得未来 SpaceX 的地位是不可撼动的（甚至不论英伟达如何）。因为在建设算力中心这件事上，之前的 xAI 已经证明了自己的能力。如果在五年这个周期内，SpaceX 开始批量在太空近地轨道建立太空算力中心，那我觉得对于其他所有 AI 公司来说，这都将是碾压一般的地位。

text:
我表弟三月份在物流中心卸货，工资8000一个月，管两顿饭。加上他一共五个人。

五个人的工资都一样的。

闲暇的时候大伙还能吹吹牛逼，玩玩手机。

四月份的时候一个50岁的大哥从车上摔了下来，回家休息去了。

后来一直没来，本来五个人的活，变成了四个人。

四个人干五个人的活，基本上就没有歇的时候，看老板的意思，也不打算加人了。

大家私底下都抱怨，工资一分钱没加，大家都不敢出头，就叫我表弟去说，我表弟是个愣头青，直接去老板办公室了，老板最后的意思说一个人加300块钱。

以后就你们四个人干了，当然也没有休息。

回去后，大家提议罢工，四个人明天都不来了。

结果就我表弟一个人没去，其他三个人第二天都去了。

因为第二天我表弟没去上班，被开除了。

后来就变成五个人的活，他们三个人干了，至于给他们加了多少钱，不得而知。

text:
Forbes 最近那篇关于硅谷“高级 nerdy escort”的文章里，提到不少客户来自 Nvidia 等大厂。

这让我想起一段非常硅谷的旧事。

我单身时，曾经和一个 Nvidia 工程师吃过一次饭。说是约会，其实也就是见面吃饭。

整顿饭，他除了不断恭维我的外貌，就是倾诉自己在约会市场上的各种不顺：女生不理解他，女生太挑，女生总是不给他机会。

我礼貌回应，但心里已经默默把他划掉了。

后来他又约过我几次，我都很客气地婉拒。没有 ghosting，没有羞辱，没有伤害他的自尊，只是正常表达“不合适”。

结果圣诞节前后，他又来约我。被我再次拒绝后，突然破防，开始对我破口大骂：

“You are not even that pretty!”

然后是一连串输出，大意是：你们这些女生都以为自己很特别，其实也不过如此；你能遇到我，应该是你的福气。

我当时立刻拉黑 - what a loser!

本来以为故事到这里就结束了。

后来我气不过，跟闺蜜 Jane 吐槽。Jane 当时也单身，也在湾区约会市场里艰难筛选。她听着听着，突然愣住，问我：“这个人叫什么？”

我们一对名字，竟然发现——她也约会过同一个人。

而且，她也经历过类似的情绪失控和攻击。

再后来，有一天 Jane 又来找我吐槽：这个人突然很神经质地给她发了一张照片，照片里是他和一个亚裔女生，配文是：

“Me and my wife.”

那种语气，不像分享幸福，更像是迟来的炫耀和报复：你看，我也有人要。

我们当时只觉得荒诞。

这当然不代表所有 Nvidia 员工，也不代表所有硅谷工程师。硅谷有很多善良、优秀、真诚的人。

但它确实暴露了这里一个不那么体面的侧面：在男多女少、高收入、高竞争、高孤独感的环境里，一部分人把亲密关系当成证明自我价值的战场。被拒绝，不是反思匹配问题，而是立刻转化为羞辱、攻击和怨恨。

所以当 Forbes 写到那些高级 escort，陪 nerds 聊聊天、哄一哄、提供情绪价值，就能收几千美元一小时的时候，我一点也不惊讶。

表面上看，这是性与金钱的交易。

更深处，是硅谷巨大的孤独、生存焦虑、性别失衡、情感贫瘠，以及一部分“精英男性”无法面对被拒绝的脆弱自尊。

这才是冰山下面更黑暗、也更值得讨论的部分。

text:
没想到华为还真是中国第一个做大模型啊？？

只不过不是大家以为什么气象模型，而是真的是Encoder-Decoder这样架构的LLM。

华为云的官网有一片2022年的文章，采访的是当时华为云人工智能领域首席科学家田奇。

2020年夏天GPT-3的出现，让欧美AI界对预训练大模型的兴趣大增。
但在国内，产业界对NLP预训练大模型的关注还相对较少。而机器视觉领域的预训练大模型，在全球范围内更是十分陌生的新鲜事物。

2020年3月，田奇加入华为云后便开始组建团队，并且进行了方向梳理。
8月，团队迎来新的核心专家。
9月，团队开始推动盘古大模型的立项，希望能够在华为云的产业基座上，完成适配各个产业AI开发的大模型。
1月，盘古大模型在华为云内部立项成功，并完成了与合作伙伴、高校的合作搭建。

2021年4月，盘古大模型正式对外发布。
其中，盘古NLP大模型作为业界首个1100亿参数的中文预训练大模型，在CLUE打榜中实现了业界领先（后在2021年5月：升级至2000亿参数的"鹏程·盘古"版本）。
为了训练NLP大模型，团队在训练过程中使用了40TB的文本数据，包含了大量的通用知识与行业经验。

同时还发布了盘古CV大模型。
盘古CV大模型也在业界首次实现了模型的按需抽取，可以在不同部署场景下抽取出不同大小的模型，动态范围可根据需求调整，从特定的小场景到综合性的复杂大场景均能覆盖。
同时，其提出的基于样本相似度的对比学习，实现了在ImageNet上小样本学习能力上的业界第一。

但中国第一个完成备案的大模型是百度文心🤔

华为云的官网有一片2022年的文章，采访的是当时华为云人工智能领域首席科学家田奇。

2020年夏天GPT-3的出现，让欧美AI界对预训练大模型的兴趣大增。
但在国内，产业界对NLP预训练大模型的关注还相对较少。而机器视觉领域的预训练大模型，在全球范围内更是十分陌生的新鲜事物。

2020年3月，田奇加入华为云后便开始组建团队，并且进行了方向梳理。
8月，团队迎来新的核心专家。
9月，团队开始推动盘古大模型的立项，希望能够在华为云的产业基座上，完成适配各个产业AI开发的大模型。
1月，盘古大模型在华为云内部立项成功，并完成了与合作伙伴、高校的合作搭建。

2021年4月，盘古大模型正式对外发布。
其中，盘古NLP大模型作为业界首个1100亿参数的中文预训练大模型，在CLUE打榜中实现了业界领先（后在2021年5月：升级至2000亿参数的"鹏程·盘古"版本）。
为了训练NLP大模型，团队在训练过程中使用了40TB的文本数据，包含了大量的通用知识与行业经验。

同时还发布了盘古CV大模型。
盘古CV大模型也在业界首次实现了模型的按需抽取，可以在不同部署场景下抽取出不同大小的模型，动态范围可根据需求调整，从特定的小场景到综合性的复杂大场景均能覆盖。
同时，其提出的基于样本相似度的对比学习，实现了在ImageNet上小样本学习能力上的业界第一。

但中国第一个完成备案的大模型是百度文心🤔

text:
今天见了一个做量化的老朋友，一年多没见，聊完有点被刺激到。

他们挖因子已经全面用大模型了。Claude Code、Codex、Hermes，整个团队在生产环节里跑起来了。不是"听说过"，不是"试了试"，是真在用。

我一直以为量化圈还在传统机器学习那个范式里，没想到他们切得这么快。

仔细想想也合理——搞投资的人对新技术的嗅觉就是比搞技术的人还灵。因为他们的反馈循环太短了：这个工具能不能帮我多挖出几个有效因子，跑一轮模拟盘就知道了。不需要开会讨论、不需要写方案、不需要说服老板，直接上手验证，有效就留，没效就换。

反倒是很多互联网公司，工具链齐全、技术能力不差，但采用新东西的速度比金融圈慢一大截。差在哪？差在反馈循环太长，试错成本被组织流程放大了。

我个人的感受就是，中国中产在消费欲望上跟美国人完全不是一个量级，根本没法比

我觉得国内50万年薪，和美国30万美元年薪，其实基本处在同一个社会收入层级。

国内年薪50万的人，几乎没有什么放纵式的享受型消费。
顶多就是买台三四十万的车，每年出门旅游一两趟，日常带家人偶尔下下馆子，不会在爱好和享乐上花太多钱

我认识的美国人里面，有不少属于年薪30万美金的群体，我感觉绝大部分人普遍是把玩当成人生第一目标，特别舍得为个人爱好砸钱

玩机车的，家里能囤五六台改装重机；玩音乐的，收藏一堆吉他、黑胶唱片堆得满满当当；玩模型的，半个车库摆满军舰、机甲模型，看得我口水横流；钓鱼佬买小游艇，买拖车，那更是我们想都不敢想的。

除此之外，几乎人人都会海外度假、玩野营，玩各种体育项目，讲的就是一个及时行乐

仔细一想，你愿意每年拿30万出来玩，在国内也能玩得这么开心，甚至更开心，但是这样的中国人，我一个都没见过

反过来，像我们这样克制的生活，攒钱买房的美国人，也许有，但我也是一个都没见过

text:
现在顶级 AI 实验室的入场券，早就不只是有学术光环了！

最近看到一篇很硬核的 ML 面试复盘文章，作者拿到了 DeepMind 等多家顶级 AI 公司的 offer，文章里面有个很现实的观察：

哪怕你手里有多篇 AI 顶会的一作，简历也只是把你送进面试间。

在真正面试时，很多考官并不会围着你的论文细节聊太久，他们更关心的是：你能不能在有限时间里写出 Transformer 的 backward pass，能不能把基础数学讲清楚，能不能现场手撕算法题。

这背后作者讲出了很残酷的行业逻辑：顶级 AI 研究员面试，很多时候筛的不是你的科研上限，而是你的工程、数学和 coding 下限。

所以顶尖博士面试前也会焦虑，也要刷题、模拟、补基础。学术成果证明你有潜力，但面试流程要确认你能稳定交付。

这也挺反直觉的：做研究像艺术，找工作却像工程。论文、idea、创造力当然重要，但真正进门时，还是要过一套非常标准化、非常具体、甚至有点像高考的筛选流程。

另外，文章里对初创公司期权的提醒也很现实：别只听估值故事，税收、流动性、行权成本和退出不确定性，都会让纸面财富和真实收益差很远。

在今天的 AI 行业，别指望靠过去的学术功劳簿一路通关。

想进顶级实验室，最好提前把面试当成一个工程项目来准备：刷题、推公式、复盘论文、模拟面试，一项项补齐。

所以顶尖博士面试前也会焦虑，也要刷题、模拟、补基础。学术成果证明你有潜力，但面试流程要确认你能稳定交付。

这也挺反直觉的：做研究像艺术，找工作却像工程。论文、idea、创造力当然重要，但真正进门时，还是要过一套非常标准化、非常具体、甚至有点像高考的筛选流程。

另外，文章里对初创公司期权的提醒也很现实：别只听估值故事，税收、流动性、行权成本和退出不确定性，都会让纸面财富和真实收益差很远。

在今天的 AI 行业，别指望靠过去的学术功劳簿一路通关。

想进顶级实验室，最好提前把面试当成一个工程项目来准备：刷题、推公式、复盘论文、模拟面试，一项项补齐。

text:
一堆人看完晚点的新闻后，臭骂“钉钉太傻逼了，无招这个人简直不拿人当人”，

然而这些年从来没一个钉钉的程序员公开表态，说过“无招这个人太傻逼了，太压榨我，给我的工资和环境完全对不起我的才华、能力、报复、规划，所以我选择直接辞职，直接跳槽到XXX拿两倍工资躺平养老”。

本质上这就是行业现状 ，我反复告诉你们，你完全可以说钉钉和无招是阿里蛀虫，浪费了整个阿里集团巨大的财务成本，做了一堆没用的东西出来，是决策层的重大失误。

但是对于绝大多数不愿意跳槽且愿意极限式管理的人而言，能够经历几轮promotion到今天的位置，手里拿这个钱，是完全不敢跳槽的，也绝对说不出“阿里对不起我，我值更多的钱，我值得更好的环境，我辞职了是你们钉钉重大的损失”这种话出来。

你拿着一两百万人民币的现金，如果不愿意干，觉得自己受到了莫大的委屈和羞辱，大可以辞职走人，去100万刀的OpenAI舒舒服服躺平，或者把整个钉钉部门裁掉，给钉钉的员工们一个伟大的、一拍两散的自由，不要耽误他们在其他地方继续发光发热。

无招谁都对不起，唯独没有对不起钉钉的这些员工。

text:
want to point out a few really interesting things here

1. Claude Code is actually the worst performing harness when using the same model, significantly behind opencode and cursor cli

this is the core reason i've been against the LLM companies focusing their business on locking people into their harness

what they are good at is making great models. they suck at making good harness products, just like how power plants won't make the best dishwashers, and how internet providers won't make the best phones

if anthropic wants to do what's best for their users, they should let people use their subscriptions in whatever harness they choose, not locked into claude code alone

2. fable 5 max is only 1pt above gpt 5.5 xhigh (77 vs 76)

this matches my experience so far - fable 5 does have the big model smell and it's pretty good, but it's not a massive jump forward like their marketing suggested, at least not on building software

this is actually alarming for anthropic because it's very unlikely people will want to pay 2x higher cost for the 1pt difference. my speculation would be that in enterprises people will be restricted to adopt fable & mythos only on some mission critical tasks, not used at scale

quotedTweet.text:
We've updated the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index, replacing SWE-Bench Pro with Datacurve's DeepSWE benchmark - the swap lifts Codex with GPT-5.5 (xhigh) above Claude Code with Opus 4.8 (max), while the newly released Claude Fable 5 (max) in Claude Code debuts at the top

DeepSWE, built by @datacurve, writes its tasks from scratch rather than adapting them from public GitHub issues or pull requests, so no model has seen the solutions during training. That matters because SWE-Bench Pro, the benchmark it replaces in our Coding Agent Index, had grown gameable, with some models recovering the fix from the repository's commit history instead of solving the task.

The swap reorders the index: Codex with GPT-5.5 (xhigh) rises from 65 to 76, overtaking Claude Code with Opus 4.8 (max) at 73. Claude Code with Fable 5 (max), which enters directly on the refreshed index, leads at 77. SWE-Bench Pro had been flattering some combinations and penalizing others.

More below.

if anthropic wants to do what's best for their users, they should let people use their subscriptions in whatever harness they choose, not locked into claude code alone

2. fable 5 max is only 1pt above gpt 5.5 xhigh (77 vs 76)

this matches my experience so far - fable 5 does have the big model smell and it's pretty good, but it's not a massive jump forward like their marketing suggested, at least not on building software

this is actually alarming for anthropic because it's very unlikely people will want to pay 2x higher cost for the 1pt difference. my speculation would be that in enterprises people will be restricted to adopt fable & mythos only on some mission critical tasks, not used at scale

We've updated the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index, replacing SWE-Bench Pro with Datacurve's DeepSWE benchmark - the swap lifts Codex with GPT-5.5 (xhigh) above Claude Code with Opus 4.8 (max), while the newly released Claude Fable 5 (max) in Claude Code debuts at the top

DeepSWE, built by @datacurve, writes its tasks from scratch rather than adapting them from public GitHub issues or pull requests, so no model has seen the solutions during training. That matters because SWE-Bench Pro, the benchmark it replaces in our Coding Agent Index, had grown gameable, with some models recovering the fix from the repository's commit history instead of solving the task.

The swap reorders the index: Codex with GPT-5.5 (xhigh) rises from 65 to 76, overtaking Claude Code with Opus 4.8 (max) at 73. Claude Code with Fable 5 (max), which enters directly on the refreshed index, leads at 77. SWE-Bench Pro had been flattering some combinations and penalizing others.

How? Last summer, after Bayern failed to sign priority target Nico Williams, they turned to alternatives. One of them was Dortmund's Jamie Gittens. A club employee was tasked with contacting Niko Kovač to get an honest opinion from him about Gittens. Kovač is said to have made it more than clear that he considers the Englishman "not professional enough" to succeed at FC Bayern. The club then abandoned the pursuit of Gittens and went all in on Luis Díaz. Gittens ended up joining Chelsea

text:
所有人都在怕 SpaceX 吸血美股，但历史已经回答过这个问题了。

今天 SPCX 上市，750 亿美元融资，1.75 万亿估值，史上最大 IPO。

我刷了一天评论，恐慌情绪只有一个：这么大盘子进来，美股的流动性要被抽干了？

我翻了历史。

2019 年 12 月，沙特阿美上市，294 亿，当时全球最大 IPO。

之后 S&P 500 没跌——一路涨到 2020 年 2 月历史高点。后来那次暴跌是 COVID，和阿美没有半毛钱关系。

2014 年 9 月，阿里巴巴纽交所挂牌，218 亿，当时也是"史上最大"。首日涨 38%。

之后 10 月 S&P 500 跌了将近 7%——这波确实发生在 BABA 上市后，看上去很像"吸血"。

但当时的真实原因是：欧洲衰退预期 + 埃博拉疫情恐慌 + 美联储缩表。BABA 只是撞上了。跌完之后，S&P 500 年底收正。

两次最大 IPO，都没引发崩盘。一次都没有。

根源上，"吸血论"的逻辑就是错的。全球股票流动性不是一个固定的水缸——SpaceX 舀走 750 亿，其他股票就少 750 亿，这个推理不成立。

机构参与大型 IPO 用的是专属的新股预算，不会去砍手里的持仓。而且为了买 SPCX，全球资金会换美元进场，这对美股是净增量，不是存量分流。

但 SpaceX 的风险是真实存在的，只不过不是你以为的那个。

94 倍市销率。2025 年净亏近 50 亿。马斯克同时掌着 Tesla、X、xAI 和 SpaceX。366 天后锁定期到期，还有一波解禁压力。

你真正需要想的问题不是"SpaceX 会不会搞垮美股"—，历史已经告诉你，不会。

你需要想的是：在 94 倍 P/S 的位置追进去，出问题的是谁。

总的来说，Fable 5 找出了一堆问题，GPT 5.5 在认的过程中，也找出了 Fable 5 不准确的地方，Fable 5 也承认 GPT 修正的是对的。

换个角度说，Fable 5 的性价比能和 GPT 5.5 比吗？我看悬。

text:
我住的小区电梯很慢

每次都能碰到一个女的，她总对我笑。

我以为她对我有意思，有一天鼓起勇气要微信。

她拒绝了，说：

“别误会，我是这栋楼的保洁

你每天扔的垃圾分类很规范，我感谢你。”

我尴尬死了。

后来我每天故意把垃圾分类做得更细。

三个月后她加了我微信

说：“你是我见过最认真的男人，我注意你很久了。”

现在我们结婚了。

婚礼上她说：“其实我第一天就看上你了

说我是保洁是骗你的，我是这栋楼的业主

就想看看你会不会因为身份改变态度。”

我笑了：“那我也骗了你

我每天分类垃圾是因为我强迫症，不是因为你。”

因为你没有衰老过。

25岁的人，人人看不起自己当年学临床的同学，自己一个个985本科毕业直接进科技互联网大厂拿高薪，临床的同学还在规培，穷得跟个王八蛋似的，

40岁的人，人人都羡慕当年学临床的同学，自己开始遇到职业瓶颈和中年危机了，临床博士们一个个在一二线城市头部大三甲升主任了， 开始进入职业快速上升期。

18~30岁，临床的人在狠狠啃书、见习、规培，30岁~40岁积累了10年一线门诊、住院医、手术经验，40岁到70岁都是人生的黄金时期。

这时候你在一家一二线城市的头部大三甲，掌握着绝对垄断、绝对稀缺的临床专业知识，

在一个1000万~3亿人辐射范围内的区域医疗中心，你掌握着几百个精细划分小专科里某个小专科的100%绝对权威，绝对决策权，唯一解释权，你一个人垄断了所有资源。

你是可以真正知识变现、资源变现、社会关系变现、人脉变现的。

同时你开始大批大批带学生，开始有大量学术产出，有大量社会和学术工作，开始出席大量医院中高层行政管理工作，要抽时间帮助建设投资几个亿的新院区，开始建设学科，开始主导省市一级别的卫健委咨询和规划工作。

同时40岁你根本不会变老，因为其他行业40岁已经没有优势了，而你40岁开始，所有的经验、经历、吃苦、资源、关系，全都成为你下一步的事业加速器，你能调度的博士生资源、社会资源、行政资源、学术资源都在显著变多。

你会越来越年轻。

text:
Developer lifecycle:

In 2015, writing code by hand was a win.
In 2019, knowing React was a win.
In 2020, knowing the latest framework was a win.
In 2021, using low-code was a win.
In 2022, using GitHub Copilot was a win.
In 2023, copy pasting code from ChatGPT was a win.
In 2025, using Codex or Claude Code was a win.
In 2026, running agents in parallel is a win.
In 2027, using AI cheaply will be a win.

Then AI gets too expensive.

In 2028, copy pasting code from ChatGPT is a win.
In 2029, using GitHub Copilot is a win.
In 2030, using low-code is a win.
In 2031, knowing the latest framework is a win.
In 2032, knowing React is a win.
In 2033, writing code by hand is a win.

text:
每周五早上，Codex都会发布本周重大更新。

今天这波更新，绝对是爬虫和逆向工程党的狂欢：Chrome 插件新增 Developer Mode，Codex 可以直接接管 Chrome DevTools 的整套能力。

我拿它分析了一遍 DeepSeek 官网聊天记录的加载逻辑。Codex 自己打开页面、监听网络请求、追踪数据流，很快发现历史消息根本不是从服务端实时拉取的。接着顺藤摸瓜，定位到本地 IndexedDB 缓存，又反向阅读网页 Bundle 里的 JS 代码，最终把聊天记录的存储、读取、恢复流程全部还原出来。

以前这种活得自己开 DevTools、翻请求、扒源码、打断点。现在一句话丢给 Codex，它自己干完了。

text:
带大家认识一下 @SpaceX 背后的女人 - Gwynne Shotwell！ 

如果说 Elon Musk 代表了 SpaceX 最疯狂、最外放、最具有戏剧性的愿景，那么 Gwynne Shotwell 就是那个把愿景一点点变成现实的人。

她是 SpaceX 长期的总裁兼 COO，也是这家公司最关键、却相对低调的灵魂人物之一。

她加入 SpaceX 的故事，本身就很有戏剧性。

2002 年，Shotwell 还在一家小型航天公司 Microcosm 工作。经同事介绍，她见到了刚刚创办 SpaceX 的 Elon Musk。

当时的 SpaceX 还非常早期，商务拓展工作甚至是由外部承包商在做。Shotwell 见到 Musk 后很直接地说：你需要一个全职负责 business development 的人。

马斯克听完，觉得有道理，就把这份工作给了她。

但 Shotwell 反而犹豫了。她想了好几个星期，没有马上答应。

直到某天下午，她堵在洛杉矶的车流里，突然想通了。她打电话给 马斯克的助理，说自己决定加入 SpaceX，并且为自己拖了这么久感到抱歉 - 她甚至开玩笑说，自己之前真是个 “f---ing idiot”。

Musk 听了大笑，也非常高兴她终于答应。

2002 年 9 月，Gwynne Shotwell 正式加入 SpaceX，成为公司最早期的核心成员之一，担任商务拓展副总裁。

后来证明，这个决定改变了她的一生，也改变了 SpaceX 的命运。

（真的就是应了我之前引用的Sheryl Sandberg的硅谷名言 - 当你被邀请上一艘飞船时，赶紧上，不要问位置在哪里！）

SpaceX 早年并不光鲜。Falcon 1 接连失败，公司资金紧张，几乎走到悬崖边。

真正拯救 SpaceX 的关键转折点之一，是 2008 年 NASA 那份价值 16 亿美元的国际空间站补给合同。

Shotwell 在其中扮演了核心角色。

这份合同不仅给 SpaceX 带来了现金流，更重要的是带来了信誉。一个曾经被很多传统航天人看不起的创业公司，终于拿到了 NASA 的正式认可。

不久之后，Musk 提拔她为 SpaceX 总裁。后来，她成为总裁兼 COO，长期掌管公司的商业、运营和执行。

很多人说，她是 SpaceX 的 “glue” - 把公司粘合在一起的人。

Shotwell 最有名的一句话，是她谈到如何和 Musk 共事：

“When Elon says something, you have to pause and not immediately blurt out, ‘Well, that’s impossible.’”

当 Elon 提出一个看似疯狂的想法时，你需要冷静停一下，不要第一反应就说：“这不可能。”

这就是她异于常人的地方。她会思考：如果这件事真的要做成，路径是什么？难点在哪里？资源怎么调？时间怎么压缩？团队怎么组织？

她既不是盲目崇拜 Musk 的执行者，也不是习惯性说“不可能”的传统管理者。她更像是 Musk 和现实世界之间的桥梁：一边理解疯狂愿景的价值，一边把它拆解成可执行的工程、商业和组织系统。

而且，Shotwell 并不是那种只坐在办公室看报表的高管。

据和她共事过的人说，她经常会走进工厂、任务控制中心和工程现场，问非常具体、甚至让人有点紧张的问题。

例如： 制造流程哪里卡住了？
宇航员训练模拟出了什么问题？
某个系统为什么这样设计？
某个环节为什么不能更快？

她不是只问战略方向，而是真的深入细节。

这也是为什么她能在 SpaceX 从一家小公司成长为全球最重要的航天公司之一的过程中，始终保持强大的运营掌控力。

有意思的是，Shotwell 还曾经提到，她很欣赏 Musk 的一个细节：他不仅关心火箭能不能飞，也关心工厂和工作空间是否足够美。

Musk 认为，工厂不应该只是冷冰冰的生产线，也应该是能激发人的空间。

Shotwell 说，在加入 SpaceX 之前，她从来没有认真想过物理环境对人的影响。但和 Musk 共事后，她开始意识到，美感、空间和人的创造力之间，其实有很深的关系。

她也曾形容 Musk 是一个很有幽默感的人。

这听起来很反差。

外界看到的 Musk，常常是低情商，极端、强势、争议不断、难以预测的。而 Shotwell 看到的，则是另一个更复杂的版本：有疯狂要求，也有极高标准；有不可思议的想象力，也有对细节近乎偏执的关注。

过去 20 多年里，Musk 身边来来去去无数高管。很多人在他的高压节奏下离开。但 Gwynne Shotwell 留了下来。

她从 SpaceX 最早期一路走到今天，见证了 Falcon 1 的失败，Falcon 9 的成功，NASA 合同的突破，Dragon 飞船，Starlink，以及 SpaceX 成为全球商业航天领域最重要的公司。

最近几年，她也越来越多站到台前。

她为 Starlink 公开发声，在国际会议上演讲，与各国政策制定者沟通，也开始谈到 AI 数据中心带来的能源需求等更宏观的话题。

但即便如此，她的公众形象依然远比 Musk 低调。

她不是那个在社交媒体上制造风暴的人，但她可能是 SpaceX 最不可替代的人之一。

如果说 Musk 负责把目标定到火星，那么 Shotwell 负责让团队相信：好，我们先把下一枚火箭发上去。

这类女性领导者特别值得被看见。

她们不一定最喜欢站在聚光灯中心，但她们能把混乱变成秩序，把愿景变成路径，把天才的疯狂转化为组织的执行力。

Gwynne Shotwell 的故事提醒我们：真正伟大的公司，往往不只是靠一个 visionary 建起来的，还需要一个能把愿景落地的人。

而 SpaceX 背后的这个女人，正是这样的人。

鹅腿阿姨是最理解“这个世界都是草台班子”的人。

鹅腿阿姨在当年爆火之后，接受了北大的专访，被人民日报报道，成为了一个励志的正面典型，同时也赚的盆满钵满。

You waited and Claude Fable 5 is finally here.

It's Mythos-class and the most capable model we've ever GA'd, and we're inviting you to be amongst the first to build with it.

We believe powerful AI can compress decades of progress into years - disease eradication, massive GDP acceleration, life extension - but AI doesn't do any of that on its own. 

People do.

Edison once said "genius is 1% inspiration and 99% perspiration" but that ratio is inverting. 

The perspiration is getting automated.

Humans have ideas. 
Agents implement, test, and evaluate them an order of magnitude faster than before.

It's becoming clear that much of what advances the frontier is automatable and progress is mostly a function of tools and resources: 
-how fast you can run experiments
-how many at once
-how quickly you get answers

Every important technology became important because someone picked it up early and aimed it at a problem that mattered.

This Saturday, June 13th, with our friends at @cerebral_valley in SF, we're giving you a day to do exactly that.

Pick up the problem that's been nagging at you and do something about it.

It will be a day of building and learning with @AnthropicAI co-founder Jared Kaplan, Research PM Jeremy Hadfield, and technical leaders from @Replit, @periodiclabs, and @_hex_tech.

With over $150K in Claude credits for winners, this is the day you go after: 
-the idea you've been sitting on
-the broken workflow in your industry
-the tool you wish existed

The longer and more complex the task, the better.

Come build something that matters and we'll see you in person on Saturday 👇

text:
These are the most relevant takeaways from a series of off-the-radar podcasts we listened to in March. Full references below. 

1. "Everyone Has Claude Now — So What's Left?"
The AI conversation moved past the demo. March was about what survives commoditization.

The most pointed frame came from Dan Shipper, who asked the question everyone's dancing around: what happens when everyone has Claude? Once the model is a utility, your moat is whatever you feed it — data and distribution — not the AI itself (Big Ideas).

Julian Bek turned that into a sales doctrine: sell against the model, not in its line of sight. If a chatbot can answer your buyer's question for free, you don't have a business — you have a feature waiting to be absorbed (TBPN).

Bret Taylor went further out on the timeline, arguing most interactions will eventually originate from agents rather than humans clicking buttons — which quietly upends how you design product, pricing, and even your homepage (Cheeky Pint).

Greg Isenberg is already living it, using MCP as a de facto sales team — agents that qualify and close (Startup Ideas). And Dan Martell dropped the stat that keeps this from feeling inevitable: only 5% of LLM users actually pay. The monetization curve has barely begun (Open Residency).

The sober counterweight: Mark Cuban doesn't think humanoid robots will last (TBPN), a useful reminder that not every AI-adjacent bet ages well.

2. The Boring-Business Goldrush
Roll-ups stopped being a finance-Twitter hobby and started looking like the cleanest AI arbitrage going.

The poster child: Corey Mullins took $25k into a $3.2M HVAC business by buying, building, and selling (Acquiring Minds). Unglamorous, repeatable, real.

Chris Koerner sized the opportunity bluntly — 800k management consultants in the US — the kind of labor pool that looks very different once AI eats the routine 80% (My First Million). Kaido Veske pointed at the same dynamic across the Atlantic, flagging a genuine gap in European PE (Buyers and Builders).

The tactical gem came from Ethan Wright: day one after closing, you call the existing customers. The book you just bought is the goldmine — most operators sleep on it (Owned and Operated).

This isn't fringe anymore. Blackstone is closing on Champions and Jake Gress is now running Goettl — institutional capital is in the trades (Service Business Mastery; To the Point). And Lacey Wilmer's origin story — her father "fell into" SMB ownership — captures how much of this world is accidental inheritance someone finally chose to take seriously (Builders and Buyers).

3. Distribution Is the Last Real Moat
Software depreciates. Audience compounds. The creators figured this out first.

Lenny Rachitsky is the proof of patience: a newsletter started in 2019 is now 1.2M subscribers and a top-10 tech podcast (Lenny's Podcast). Matt McGarry narrowed the whole game to three channels worth defending — YouTube, email, and podcast (New Media).

Lara Acosta showed the personal-brand-to-product flywheel paying out: $300k MRR across a vacation tool and Kleo (Personal IPO). The mechanics aren't mysterious — David Walsh's formula is just "write good content, and humor wins" (Founder's Story).

The investor's version of this thesis came from Chetan Puttagunta, who put the application-layer shift on par with on-prem → cloud (The Peel). Translation for builders: the audience you compound now is the distribution you'll wish you had when software gets cheap to clone.

4. The Operator's Mindset
Quieter than the AI noise, but the part that actually compounds — and a flag for advisors paying attention.

Adrian Aoun's line is the whole ethos: founders will things into action — agency is the scarce input (Summation). Chad Hladczuk's frame is the practical companion: most decisions are two-way doors, so act faster (The Peel). And Marc Andreessen's advice is almost rude in its simplicity — don't be introspective, move on (David Senra).

The most self-aware comment of the month belongs to Lee Yoder: "I like real estate because I'm not that smart or creative and there are economies of scale." Structural advantage beats cleverness (Wealthy Entrepreneur).

For RIAs, two episodes deserve a bookmark. Peter Mallouk reframed the actual product as peace of mind, not returns (RIA Edge). These are the most relevant takeaways from a series of off-the-radar podcasts we listened to in March. Full references below. 

1. "Everyone Has Claude Now — So What's Left?"
The AI conversation moved past the demo. March was about what survives commoditization.

The most pointed frame came from Dan Shipper, who asked the question everyone's dancing around: what happens when everyone has Claude? Once the model is a utility, your moat is whatever you feed it — data and distribution — not the AI itself (Big Ideas).

Julian Bek turned that into a sales doctrine: sell against the model, not in its line of sight. If a chatbot can answer your buyer's question for free, you don't have a business — you have a feature waiting to be absorbed (TBPN).

Bret Taylor went further out on the timeline, arguing most interactions will eventually originate from agents rather than humans clicking buttons — which quietly upends how you design product, pricing, and even your homepage (Cheeky Pint).

Greg Isenberg is already living it, using MCP as a de facto sales team — agents that qualify and close (Startup Ideas). And Dan Martell dropped the stat that keeps this from feeling inevitable: only 5% of LLM users actually pay. The monetization curve has barely begun (Open Residency).

The sober counterweight: Mark Cuban doesn't think humanoid robots will last (TBPN), a useful reminder that not every AI-adjacent bet ages well.

2. The Boring-Business Goldrush
Roll-ups stopped being a finance-Twitter hobby and started looking like the cleanest AI arbitrage going.

The poster child: Corey Mullins took $25k into a $3.2M HVAC business by buying, building, and selling (Acquiring Minds). Unglamorous, repeatable, real.

Chris Koerner sized the opportunity bluntly — 800k management consultants in the US — the kind of labor pool that looks very different once AI eats the routine 80% (My First Million). Kaido Veske pointed at the same dynamic across the Atlantic, flagging a genuine gap in European PE (Buyers and Builders).

The tactical gem came from Ethan Wright: day one after closing, you call the existing customers. The book you just bought is the goldmine — most operators sleep on it (Owned and Operated).

This isn't fringe anymore. Blackstone is closing on Champions and Jake Gress is now running Goettl — institutional capital is in the trades (Service Business Mastery; To the Point). And Lacey Wilmer's origin story — her father "fell into" SMB ownership — captures how much of this world is accidental inheritance someone finally chose to take seriously (Builders and Buyers).

3. Distribution Is the Last Real Moat
Software depreciates. Audience compounds. The creators figured this out first.

Lenny Rachitsky is the proof of patience: a newsletter started in 2019 is now 1.2M subscribers and a top-10 tech podcast (Lenny's Podcast). Matt McGarry narrowed the whole game to three channels worth defending — YouTube, email, and podcast (New Media).

Lara Acosta showed the personal-brand-to-product flywheel paying out: $300k MRR across a vacation tool and Kleo (Personal IPO). The mechanics aren't mysterious — David Walsh's formula is just "write good content, and humor wins" (Founder's Story).

The investor's version of this thesis came from Chetan Puttagunta, who put the application-layer shift on par with on-prem → cloud (The Peel). Translation for builders: the audience you compound now is the distribution you'll wish you had when software gets cheap to clone.

4. The Operator's Mindset
Quieter than the AI noise, but the part that actually compounds — and a flag for advisors paying attention.

Adrian Aoun's line is the whole ethos: founders will things into action — agency is the scarce input (Summation). Chad Hladczuk's frame is the practical companion: most decisions are two-way doors, so act faster (The Peel). And Marc Andreessen's advice is almost rude in its simplicity — don't be introspective, move on (David Senra).

@CEOAdam @cvpayne @AMCTheatres  $AMC
Market is about to price the future. not Covid past
The pipeline for the rest of 2026 and into 2027 positions AMC for a real launch trajectory. Management (Adam Aron) has been vocal about this: they see 2026 domestic box office potentially $500M–$1.2B higher than 2025, with robust growth in H2 and international/ODEON adding extra lift. Q2 is already delivering the. https://t.co/OmRsQjGsFA (https://t.co/rZD6whiXAZ) 
Q3/Q4 2026 Outlook (Even Stronger Slate)
Q3 (July–Sept) and Q4 (Oct–Dec) have heavier event density:
•  July: Minions & Monsters, The Odyssey (Nolan), potential holdovers from Toy Story 5.
•  Later summer/fall: More family tentpoles, horror, and originals building on 2026’s diverse wins (Backrooms, Obsession, etc.).
•  Holiday Q4: Packed with franchise firepower, re-releases, and awards-season buzz.
This follows a front-loaded but strong Q2 ($3.0B–$3.3B+ domestic possible). Summer 2026 is already tracking toward record post-pandemic levels in spots, and the back half benefits from no major content gaps + growing event programming (Arena One concerts, World Cup, F1, etc.). AMC’s premium screens, concessions leverage, and international share should amplify this into outsized revenue/FCF gains. https://t.co/kGCJaENQla (https://t.co/HchvbmxcUy) 
2027: The Real Catalyst Year
Early views call 2027 potentially even bigger than 2026 — studios are ramping output with stacked franchises:
•  Avengers: Secret Wars, Frozen 3, Shrek 5, Spider-Man: Beyond the Spider-Verse, The Batman Part II, Sonic 4, Legend of Zelda adaptation, Minecraft sequel, and more.
•  Deeper recovery in theatrical windows + nostalgia/IP demand could push annual domestic toward or past pre-pandemic peaks.
AMC is expanding Dolby screens (25%+ increase by end of 2027), rolling out more experiential formats, and layering in high-margin alt-content. This diversification reduces pure box-office dependency while capturing upside from a booming slate. https://t.co/ZVNprGlq3i (https://t.co/2Qz5FseDhB) 
Financial Translation for AMC:
•  Revenue: Q2 blowout ($1.8B+ in your scenario) sets the tone. Full-year 2026 could see meaningful growth vs. 2025, with Q3/Q4 and 2027 compounding it.
•  EBIT/Adjusted EBITDA: Continued positive territory and expansion from operating leverage.
•  FCF: Path to sustainable positivity opens up as attendance scales and debt moves help. Analysts are cautious on price targets (~$2 range consensus, with outliers higher), but the operational momentum is what matters for a potential re-rating. https://t.co/yWHjXpmtWV (https://t.co/Qh6VX8Wziz) 
The setup is there: theatrical recovery has legs, AMC is the scale leader capturing it globally, and the content pipeline is loaded. Q2 earnings (early-mid August) should be a strong validation if late June holds. This isn’t just a quarter — it’s the inflection building into a multi-year run.

The fix isn't slowing down deployment. It's building the governance layer that lets you move fast without flying blind.

text:
前几天新模型发布，加上也在敲打自己的agent，也是赶巧挑了一点时间从头到尾翻看了一下Claude的技术博客，其实是有点感触的.

挑几个典型的说，比如从24年提出传统rag 的chunking再embedding和BM25会弱匹配，于是提出给每段chunking加上contextual的标签.

又到context engineering面对的困境（比如虽然window是200k，但self attention等原因会导致只要加入新的信息模型就会难以维持远距离信息的关系，太多模糊的工具会稀释模型注意力....），以及提出了渐进式披露，jit查询信息源，利用外部文件做持久化，subagent等等策略

再到长任务会context anxiety，于是设计可供agent稳定使用的脚手架（我觉得此harness非彼harness），比如在agent外部环境设计状态机，强制用代码规定agent必须按流程执行并达成目标通过测试（default fail），才能继续，而不是只把规则写在prompt里让agent自己监守自盗，以及用文件作为真相在多agent间传递信息而不是对话.........等等等等

越看其实越感觉agent现在的发展太快太快了，短短两年从初代的swe agent到现在想要自己独立写一个具有各种现代功能的agent已经很难了，特别是看着codex天天发版更是越来越感觉道阻且艰

不知道怎么说，计算机确实是这样的一个学科，但agent确实是一个很有意思的方向，还是想尽力跟进的

In the early 1990s, I was dealt a crushing blow as a grad student at the @uwyo:  a referee rejected one of my field experiments with a line I've never forgotten: "This author clearly does not understand experimental economics, which is best done in the laboratory.......I strongly advise rejecting this “field experimental” paper."

Thirty years later, a different referee (I think!) on a different paper wrote: "This author performs a field experiment, which clearly is the preferred approach..." and then: "...but I still advise rejecting the paper."

While the ultimate decision did not change, the words are indicative of a pendulum that has swung within experimental economics. Field experiments are now run at industrial scale, from Uber to Walmart to Meta, and in broader orgs, from local governments to NGOs to non-profits. One was even recently called the "single best evidence" in a major antitrust ruling. 

All of this is a very good thing. But somewhere along the way, "take it to the field" started to sound like "give up on the lab."

That's a mistake, and in a new paper titled “Don’t Give Up on Lab Experiments: Why the Field Still Needs the Lab,” I try to explain why the field needs the lab more than ever, available for free here: https://t.co/DC3QJYcPwz

My argument is a simple one. The four standard design types (lab, artefactual, framed, and natural field experiments) are not rungs on a quality ladder. They are comparative-static restrictions of one maximization problem, and each one identifies a parameter the others cannot. The natural field experiment recovers behavior in the wild, free of selection and scrutiny. The lab enforces the identification conditions the field must inherit from the market. Lose either and you are holding half the picture.

The paper also explores how more recent data generation movements fit within this structure, including online experiments, surveys, and “lab-in-the-field experiments.” The paper argues that internal and external validity are not substitutes at the level of a research program. They are complements, and the value of each rises with the other.

text:
Aligning with Your Deeper Purpose

Hey friend,

There are moments in leadership when you’re accomplishing things on the outside, but inside you feel a quiet emptiness, like you’re pushing hard but unsure if it’s still your race.

I’ve experienced that feeling myself, and I’ve heard it from many founders I work with.

Today, we’re exploring how to "Align with your Deeper Purpose", reconnecting with that inner “why” that makes all the tough days worthwhile and fuels truly sustainable leadership.

Common patterns that distract us:

• Chasing external success metrics while our core values get ignored
• Saying yes to opportunities that look good but don’t feel right
• Leading from momentum and busyness instead of purpose

Here’s the truth: When you lead from a place of deep inner alignment, everything shifts. Your decisions become clearer, your energy intensifies, and your work regains meaning.

Simple Purpose Exercise, do this today:

Take a quiet moment and ask yourself:

“If I led from my deepest values this week, what would I start doing… and what would I stop doing?”

Write down one small aligned action and commit to it. Even a tiny step counts.

This practice enhances your Clarity and Self-Worth pillars and brings you back to yourself.

The 30-Day Imposter Reset Challenge offers powerful reflection tools and alignment exercises to help you reconnect with your purpose and lead from it every day.

If you’re ready to feel more aligned and fulfilled in your leadership, comment or DM RESET below, and I’ll send you the workbook.

Question for leaders & founders:

How aligned do you currently feel between your daily work and your deeper purpose? What’s one thing that keeps you connected?

Share openly in the comments; your words could inspire someone else today.
You were meant for meaningful work.

The stronger your Inner Temple, the louder your true purpose rings.

You have everything you need inside you. Keep returning to it.

Welcome Day 21 @Aspirerfirm

Thank you for being here, and stay blessed! 

Aspire Higher. Build Firmer.

Unless the algorithm that X uses to decide what to post is public, there is a huge likelihood that Elon Musk is actually controlling the narrative. The kind of posts he puts shows his tendency to spread lies. 

If he is openly spreading lies, it it very likely that he is also surreptitiously spreading lies too. 

The one lie that has become truth for many is that declining population is a bigger threat to humanity than global warming. The population of the world will increase by 2 billion by the end of the century, and yet I see so many posts from others warning the world about declining population.

If he really cares about free speech, the algorithm should be made public just as BitCoin algorithm is public.

When the World Cup comes to the United States in the summer of 2026, it will be the first time the tournament has been played in America in 32 years. Congratulations to VEON and our Founder and Chairman Augie K Fabella II, who took home the Gold Stevie Award for Thought Leader of the Year 🏆

Bringing together some of the biggest names in business leadership in New York last night, the 24th Annual American Business Awards celebrated resilience, innovation and leadership in a rapidly changing world — making the recognition especially meaningful.

Under Augie’s Board leadership, VEON has expanded its digital ecosystems to serve nearly 230 million active users across markets that are home to over 520 million people. One of the defining milestones has been the @Nasdaq listing of @TwiyKyivstar — the first Ukrainian company ever to list on a U.S. exchange.

A proud moment for VEON, for Kyivstar, and for the teams across our markets helping turn ambitious ideas into real impact every day.

Congratulations, Augie, on a well-deserved recognition!

@TheStevieAwards

In December, a $495 phone went on sale in China for 3,499 yuan. It sold out in hours. On the resale market, it went for 43% over list.

Inside was @BytedanceTalk's AI agent. It opens apps, taps buttons, pays bills. The owner never touches the screen.

Then the platforms moved. WeChat suspended accounts that used its voice control. Alipay cut its access to payments. Taobao followed.

A machine showed up with money, and the biggest apps in China turned it away.

Who blocks a paying customer?
